findings.title: A branch name that collides with an existing tag makes a legitimately created worktree permanently unremovable and unmergeable (branch-mismatch; force has no effect). This is a regression introduced by the uncommitted N1 change.
findings.where: packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/src/git.ts -> checkedOutBranch (uses `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`) consumed by packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/src/ops.ts -> revalidateRecordedBranch (string equality `reported !== entry.branch`).
evidence: probe-ambiguity.log A: with `git tag feature` present, createWorktree({name:'alice', branch:'feature'}) returns NO-REFUSAL and records branch 'feature'; the worktree's `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` is 'heads/feature'; merge and remove(force:true) both refuse 'branch-mismatch'; the directory survives and the record stays active.

probe-ambiguity.log B: the same happens to the DEFAULT branch: with `git tag agent/alice`, createWorktree({name:'alice'}) records 'agent/alice', HEAD reports 'heads/agent/alice', and both operations refuse branch-mismatch.

probe-head-tag.log: against a git-archive copy of HEAD source (no N1 revalidation yet), the identical create+remove(force) returns NO-REFUSAL and the directory is gone -> the stranding is introduced by the uncommitted change, not pre-existing.

probe-branch-plumbing.log: inside the tag-colliding worktree, `git branch --show-current` correctly answers 'feature' while `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` answers 'heads/feature' (and strict/loose variants agree with the latter) — the fix direction.

probe-ambiguity-recovery.log: the tool still refuses 'branch-mismatch' while the directory exists; after a manual `rm -rf <worktree>` the same remove(force) prunes, deletes the branch and tombstones the record — i.e. only manual filesystem intervention recovers, not the tool.
findings.why_it_matters: remove and merge are the core lifecycle; a user who creates a branch named like an existing tag (tags and branch names commonly share names) gets a worktree the row can never merge or clean up. The registered name and the active-slot cap stay consumed; the docs' no-stranding guarantee is false. The fix must keep the HEAD-equality check but obtain the branch name from `git symbolic-ref --quiet HEAD` (strip refs/heads/; detached -> undefined) or `git branch --show-current`.
findings.fix_direction: Change checkedOutBranch to a non-abbreviating source (`git symbolic-ref --quiet HEAD`, strip the `refs/heads/` prefix, detached returns undefined; or `git branch --show-current`), keep revalidateRecordedBranch's equality rule and its detached/mismatch refusals, and add regression tests: tag 'feature' + create branch 'feature' -> remove and merge succeed; tag 'agent/alice' + default create -> remove succeeds.

findings.title: A full-ref branch spelling (refs/heads/dev) bypasses the new protected-name creation refusal and produces the same unremovable/unmergeable record; the guard compares the protected list by exact string only.
findings.where: packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/src/ops.ts -> createEntry (deps.config.protectedBranches.includes(plan.branch)) and the recorded/consumed name in src/ops.ts -> revalidateRecordedBranch / src/git.ts -> checkedOutBranch.
evidence: probe-refspelling.log: control create branch 'dev' with protectedBranches ['dev'] -> protected-branch. With the same config, create branch 'refs/heads/dev' -> NO-REFUSAL, recorded branch 'refs/heads/dev'; the worktree HEAD abbreviates to 'heads/refs/heads/dev'; merge and remove(force:true) both refuse branch-mismatch; the directory survives, the record stays active; removing the name from protectedBranches does not help.
probe-refspelling.log: the same with branch 'refs/heads/main' (not protected) -> NO-REFUSAL then branch-mismatch on both operations, so this is not only a protected-list issue.

probe-refspelling.log: branch 'refs/heads/never-existed' (no colliding local branch) round-trips ('refs/heads/never-existed') and removes successfully, isolating the trigger to the abbreviation collision.
Tool input validation: packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/src/git.ts -> isValidBranch accepts 'refs/heads/dev' (`git check-ref-format --branch` exits 0), so the public tool accepts the spelling.
Neither docs nor tool descriptions warn against refs/ spelling; the four docs' protected guarantee therefore does not hold for this spelling.
findings.why_it_matters: F4's purpose is to stop creation from admitting a record that remove/merge later refuse. A caller can still reach that stranded state through the public create tool by using a full-ref spelling; for a protected branch the new refusal is bypassed entirely. The `refs/`-rooted name also makes the downstream rev commands resolve inconsistently (branchExists prepends refs/heads/ while merge/merge-base treat it as a full rev), so simply fixing the abbreviation in F1 is not sufficient: creation-side rejection/canonicalization is required.
findings.fix_direction: Reject a branch argument rooted at `refs/` (and any name whose recorded form cannot round-trip) at createEntry before any mutation, with invalid-branch and a message naming the accepted short-branch form; add tests for 'refs/heads/dev' (existing protected branch) and 'refs/heads/main' asserting refusal with no ref/dir/registration/index. Alternatively canonicalize to the short name and prove remove/merge use the same ref everywhere, but rejection is the smaller change.

findings.title: The four docs' absolute no-stranding guarantee is stronger than the implemented and tested behaviour.
findings.where: docs/worktree.md, docs/worktree.zh-CN.md, packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/README.md, packages/mpd-worktree-plugin/README.zh-CN.md ('...so a worktree can never be created on a protected branch and then stranded by that revalidation').
evidence: F2 shows a protected branch named through its full-ref spelling is not refused at creation and is stranded by revalidation.
F1 shows a non-protected branch name colliding with a tag is created and then stranded by revalidation (the sentence's broader 'never stranded' reading).
findings.why_it_matters: The docs are part of the frozen requirement (accurate clause in all four files). Once F1/F2 are fixed, the protected-name sentence becomes true; until then it overstates the guarantee.
findings.fix_direction: No separate doc edit is required if F1/F2 are fixed as described; otherwise qualify the sentence to the literal protectedBranches entries and disclose the manual-recovery bound. Re-run verify:docs after either change.

declined_to_judge: Pre-existing records already on a now-protected branch: no migration is added; the create refusal names removing the name from protectedBranches as the recovery, and migrating records is outside the frozen creation scope. Set aside as a declared bound, not a failure of this repair.

Config change after creation that adds the record's branch to protectedBranches deliberately freezes remove/merge; the revalidation is force-blind by design and the operator owns protection. Set aside as intentional.
protectedBranches entries are not trimmed in resolveConfig, so a config value ' dev ' protects nothing: pre-existing config behaviour untouched by this diff.
Case-insensitive filesystems and Windows path handling were not exercised; the review is Linux-only.
Ambiguity with refs other than tags (remote-tracking refs, notes, refs/<name>) was not exhaustively enumerated; the tag case is proven and the symbolic-ref fix covers the class. Set aside as a bound.
Refusal precedence (protected-branch vs name-registered/path-exists/limit-reached) differs by pre-existing check order; all paths leave no side effect and the frozen requirement does not order them.
The reattach refusal leaves the stale record active and the name registered while protection is on; this is the intended degrade and recovery works once the name is unprotected (probe D9/D10).
Merge target force:true still bypasses target protection; unchanged and documented, not part of F4.

The pre-N1 wrong-ref merge semantics for full-ref spellings (git merge resolves the named existing branch) are blocked in the current tree by branch-mismatch; the deeper merge-semantics analysis was not separately audited beyond the evidence above.
The new tests simulate a config change by mutating the resolved config object in place; acceptable as a unit-test technique, not a production behaviour claim.
